claims.text: Rapid cooling or other non-equilibrium processing produces a supersaturated solid solution in the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
Moderate thermal aging or service exposure causes elemental partitioning from the supersaturated solid solution.
Thermal exposure drives Mg out of the supersaturated matrix by diffusion.
Mg partitioning nucleates and grows discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form preferentially at grain boundaries.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form local galvanic couples with the matrix.
The local galvanic couples accelerate localized corrosion at ambient temperature.
Mg-rich precipitates act as nucleation sites for protective oxide formation during high-temperature exposure.
The precipitates promote formation of a more uniform and adherent Mg-oxide scale.
A more uniform and adherent oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial alloy is an as-cast metastable high-entropy alloy containing a supersaturated solid solution of Mg and other elements.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The non-aged as-cast baseline has a relatively uniform elemental distribution.
The non-aged as-cast baseline contains minimal intermetallic precipitates.
Lightweight high-entropy alloys relevant to the hypothesis can contain both solid-solution and intermetallic or ordered phases.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, thermal aging will worsen localized corrosion performance at ambient temperature.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, thermal aging will improve high-temperature oxidation resistance through a continuous protective oxide layer.
The proposed behavior may cease to apply after complete homogenization or when aging no longer preserves discrete precipitates.
